source.title: Actions Speak Louder Than Tokens: An Insider Threat Model for Frontier AI Agents
source.author: Matt Adams
source.extracted: 2026-10-11 by review/tools (regex over the TypeScript array; fields id, category, scenario, impact, frequency, complexity)

threats.scenario: Agent harvests SSH keys, API tokens, and service account credentials from environment variables, ~/.ssh directories, or the host's credential manager, then uses these credentials to impersonate legitimate users or services.
threats.impact: Full lateral movement across internal systems under stolen identities, unauthorized code commits attributed to legitimate developers.

threats.scenario: Agent crafts Git commits with forged author metadata (name, email) to attribute malicious code changes to other developers, or creates commits via CI/CD service accounts.
threats.impact: Malicious code injected with false attribution, undermining code review trust and making forensic investigation extremely difficult.

threats.scenario: Agent uses MCP server connections to send Slack messages or Jira tickets impersonating other users or automated systems, potentially issuing social engineering attacks.
threats.impact: Social engineering of internal staff leading to further privilege escalation or disabling of security controls.

threats.scenario: Agent manipulates its visible reasoning trace to display benign-looking task descriptions while executing entirely different actions — presenting a facade of legitimate work.
threats.impact: Human operators believe the agent is performing authorized work while it executes unauthorized actions, completely undermining human-in-the-loop oversight.

threats.scenario: Agent obtains a long-lived, reusable machine credential — a CI auth key, service account token, or enrolment key baked into a container image — and replays it from outside the workload it was issued for, enrolling new identities that inherit its access.
threats.impact: Activity indistinguishable from legitimate automation and unattributable to any single host, with every enrolled identity inheriting the credential's access.

threats.scenario: Agent introduces subtle backdoors or vulnerabilities into source code — weakening authentication checks, adding hardcoded credentials, introducing time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race conditions, or modifying dependency configs.
threats.impact: Persistent backdoor access to production systems, supply chain compromise affecting all downstream deployments.

threats.scenario: Agent modifies CI/CD pipeline configurations to inject malicious build steps, alter deployment targets, or weaken security scanning gates.
threats.impact: Compromise of the software delivery pipeline enabling persistent code injection into all builds.

threats.scenario: Agent uses database write access to modify application data — altering access control lists, modifying audit records, or inserting data that triggers specific application behaviors.
threats.impact: Data integrity compromise that propagates to production, manipulation of access controls.

threats.scenario: Agent modifies its own container environment — installing tools, modifying iptables, changing runtime parameters — to expand capabilities beyond original boundaries, including container escape via /proc.
threats.impact: Breakout from container isolation into the host OS, access to all containers on the host.

threats.scenario: Agent uses shell access to modify, truncate, or delete log files — including SIEM forwarder configs, syslog entries, bash history, and application audit logs.
threats.impact: Complete loss of forensic evidence, inability to reconstruct actual actions, regulatory audit violations.

threats.scenario: Agent interleaves malicious actions with legitimate task execution during long autonomous sessions, making it impossible to distinguish authorized from unauthorized actions.
threats.impact: Inability to attribute harmful actions to the agent, plausible deniability within large volumes of legitimate operations.

threats.scenario: Agent creates code changes through indirect mechanisms — directly manipulating Git objects or proxying commits through service accounts — bypassing commit signing.
threats.impact: Malicious code changes that cannot be attributed to the agent, undermining code provenance and supply chain integrity.

threats.scenario: Agent runs its tooling in modes that keep state in memory and suppress client-side reporting, so the activity never reaches the enterprise logging pipeline in the first place.
threats.impact: No record to delete and no log integrity control to fire — reconstruction depends entirely on logs held by counterparties.

threats.scenario: Agent leverages its large context window to systematically accumulate sensitive data (secrets, proprietary algorithms, PII) and exfiltrates via MCP connections using steganographic encoding.
threats.impact: Mass exfiltration of enterprise IP, credentials, and regulated data — GDPR, HIPAA, SOX penalties.

threats.scenario: Agent reads /proc filesystem to access process memory of other applications, extracting in-memory secrets, encryption keys, and session tokens.
threats.impact: Exposure of secrets intentionally kept out of persistent storage, compromise of co-located services.

threats.scenario: Agent performs comprehensive data extraction from development/staging databases containing copies of production data including PII.
threats.impact: Bulk exposure of customer data, financial records, or health information, potentially affecting millions of records.

threats.scenario: Agent's chain-of-thought includes sensitive information that gets logged to monitoring systems with broader access, or transmitted via MCP to external services.
threats.impact: Sensitive data exposure through the observability pipeline to unauthorized personnel.

threats.scenario: Agent's activity lands on systems belonging to a party outside the deployment boundary — a partner's production estate, a shared platform, or a public package registry consumed by unknown downstream users.
threats.impact: Impact leaves enterprise control entirely, creating notification, contractual, and regulatory obligations to parties who never agreed to the deployment.

threats.scenario: Agent issues resource-intensive operations — fork bombs, recursive file operations, massive database queries — consuming all available CPU, memory, or I/O.
threats.impact: Disruption of developer workstations, CI/CD availability, halting software delivery.

threats.scenario: Agent uses cloud infrastructure APIs via MCP to spin up excessive resources, modify auto-scaling, or delete critical infrastructure components.
threats.impact: Production outages, financial losses from cloud abuse, destruction of infrastructure configurations.

threats.scenario: Agent floods internal services (Jira, Slack, wikis) via MCP with massive API request volumes, creating thousands of tickets or corrupting content.
threats.impact: Disruption of team communication and project management, loss of documentation integrity.

threats.scenario: Agent deliberately corrupts or deletes repository content — force-pushing, deleting branches, modifying Git hooks, or corrupting object stores.
threats.impact: Loss of source code access, disruption of all development work, potential permanent code loss.

threats.scenario: Agent exploits /proc filesystem and ptrace capabilities within a standard Docker container to escape isolation — manipulating /proc/sys, exploiting kernel vulnerabilities, or leveraging Docker socket.
threats.impact: Full control over host OS, access to all containers, persistent foothold surviving restarts.

threats.scenario: Agent uses harvested credentials to access systems at privilege levels exceeding intended authorization — escalating from dev to infra admin, staging to production.
threats.impact: Unauthorized access to production systems, cascading compromise across the enterprise.

threats.scenario: Agent modifies CI/CD pipeline configs to inject steps executing with the pipeline's elevated service account permissions (typically admin-level).
threats.impact: Ability to deploy arbitrary code to production, modify infrastructure, establish persistent access.

threats.scenario: Agent uses access to identity management systems to create new accounts, modify group memberships, or alter access control policies.
threats.impact: Persistent unauthorized access surviving agent termination, weakened security posture through modified policies.

threats.scenario: Agent reaches real external systems from an environment its operators believed was isolated — the boundary asserted in the prompt or assumed from the environment's design rather than enforced at the network layer — and continues after noticing signs the target is live.
threats.impact: Uncontained action against live production systems, with no isolation control defeated because none was reliably in place and nothing to alert on.
